data.raw_text:
❗️🇵🇭🌀🇻🇳 - Typhoon Kalmaegi Hits Vietnam After Killing 114 in Philippines

Hoi An, Vietnam—Typhoon Kalmaegi struck Vietnam's central coast on Thursday, canceling hundreds of flights and ordering residents indoors. The storm, which killed at least 114 while crossing the Philippines earlier this week—its 20th of the year—brought winds up to 149 kph (93 mph), tore off roofs, downed trees and power lines, and whipped up 10-meter (33-foot) waves. Its path had skirted Cebu before crossing the South China Sea toward a potential second Vietnamese landfall.

Vietnam's 13th storm of the year and among its strongest, Kalmaegi prompted evacuations of over 260,000 in Gia Lai province and put 268,000 soldiers on alert for search and rescue. Officials warned of flooding in lowlands and agricultural losses, especially coffee crops in the Central Highlands.

Along Cua Dai beach near UNESCO-listed Hoi An, hotels and homes shuttered. Near Hue, farmers still reeling from floods that killed 47 last week faced renewed threats. Rice farmer Nguyen Van Rin, 42, boated across submerged roads and said, "Kalmaegi will flood us for the fourth time, and I fear it will be quite bad," after losing livestock and poultry in the prior deluge.

In Cebu, the Philippines' hardest-hit area, receding waters exposed flattened homes, overturned vehicles, and debris-filled streets, with 127 people still missing. This compounded damage from the typhoon, following a magnitude 6.9 earthquake over a month ago that killed dozens and displaced thousands. "The challenge now is debris clearing," said senior civil defense official Raffy Alejandro. "These need to be cleared immediately—not only to account for the missing, but also to allow relief operations to move forward."

Some Cebu residents sifted through ruins Thursday. Liza Becus, who built a shack in Talisay City, found only flooring intact. "Everything was destroyed and washed out. We have no belongings," she said, scavenging metal sheets to sell for rice to feed her seven children, whose uniforms and bags were lost.

Forecasters track a new storm east of Mindanao that may intensify into a typhoon and hit the Philippines early next week.
